blind_positions.summary: Adagrasib (MRTX849, KRAZATI) is a covalent KRAS G12C inhibitor submitted under NDA 216340 for accelerated approval in adult patients with KRAS G12C-mutated locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC who have received at least one prior systemic therapy. The pivotal evidence derives from a single-arm, multicohort expansion trial (KRYSTAL-1/Study 849-001), with a primary efficacy population of 112 patients demonstrating an ORR of 43% (95% CI: 34–53%) by BICR per RECIST v1.1 and a median DOR of 8.5 months (95% CI: 6.2–13.8). The indication as sought is biomarker-selected (KRAS G12C, confirmed by FDA-approved CDx), the unmet need is substantial, and the effect size is clinically meaningful relative to available second-line options. The evidentiary package meets the statutory standard for accelerated approval under 21 CFR 314.510, with ORR serving as a surrogate endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit, consistent with FDA's published NSCLC endpoint guidance. Key reviewable concerns — single-arm trial design, dose optimization, and confirmatory trial obligations — are addressable through labeling and PMRs rather than a Complete Response Letter. No blocking regulatory deficiency is identified in this discipline.
key_concerns: Single-arm, non-randomized trial design precludes direct causal attribution of benefit and introduces known and unknown patient selection bias; no randomized confirmatory data are available at time of submission.

ORR and DOR are surrogate endpoints not validated as predictors of OS in KRAS G12C-mutated NSCLC; accelerated approval pathway requires a confirmatory trial (PMR) to verify clinical benefit per 21 CFR 314.510.

Dose optimization has not been adequately explored: 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction at 600 mg BID, suggesting the approved dose may not be optimally selected; FDA has identified this as warranting a dose-optimization PMR.

Companion diagnostic concordance: the plasma-based CDx (RESOLUTION ctDx FIRST) demonstrated only ~63% PPA versus tissue, meaning up to 37% of tissue-positive patients could be missed; labeling must require reflex to tissue testing for plasma-negative results.

Inspectional findings at Site #811 (unreported AEs: sepsis, DVT, seizure; unreported concomitant medication; failure to reconsent three patients following protocol amendment) introduce data integrity concerns, though OSI concluded overall trial conduct was adequate.

All 112 efficacy-evaluable patients had received prior platinum-based chemotherapy AND anti-PD-(L)1 therapy; the label population ('at least one prior systemic therapy') is slightly broader than the studied population, creating a minor labeling precision concern.
Confirmatory randomized trial (Study 849-012) has been committed to but not yet initiated or reported; accelerated approval is contingent on this PMR being formally required and tracked.
No patient-reported outcome (PRO) data were submitted, limiting the ability to characterize the patient experience and symptom benefit in labeling.

deficiencies.description: Absence of a randomized confirmatory trial at time of submission: The entire efficacy package rests on a single-arm expansion cohort (KRYSTAL-1 Cohort A, n=112). Under 21 CFR 314.510 and FDA's NSCLC endpoint guidance, accelerated approval based on ORR requires a PMR confirmatory trial demonstrating clinical benefit (e.g., OS or PFS improvement in a randomized setting). Study 849-012 has been committed to but not yet conducted. This is not a blocking deficiency because the accelerated approval framework explicitly anticipates this gap and the PMR mechanism is the regulatory instrument designed to address it; the ORR effect size (43%) and DOR (median 8.5 months, 58% ≥6 months) are sufficient to meet the 'reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit' standard in this high-unmet-need population.

Dose not optimized at time of approval: The 600 mg BID dose was selected without adequate comparative evaluation of alternative dose levels for efficacy-safety balance. An 82% rate of dose interruption or reduction is exceptionally high and signals that the approved dose may impose unnecessary toxicity burden. While exposure-response analyses were conducted, they do not definitively establish that 600 mg BID is the optimal dose. FDA has appropriately identified a dose-optimization PMR; this is addressable post-approval and does not constitute a blocking deficiency, but must be formally required.

Plasma CDx (RESOLUTION ctDx FIRST) positive percent agreement of ~63% versus tissue reference standard: A PPA of 63% means approximately 37% of tissue-positive (true KRAS G12C-mutant) patients would test negative by plasma and potentially be denied an effective therapy if plasma testing alone is used. This is a companion diagnostic adequacy concern with direct implications for the indicated population. It is addressable by a labeling requirement to reflex plasma-negative results to tissue testing, and CDRH has imposed postmarket study requirements on the device; it does not block approval of the drug but must be reflected in prescribing information.

blind_positions.summary: Adagrasib (KRAZATI) demonstrates a clinically meaningful objective response rate of 43% (95% CI: 34–53%) with a median duration of response of 8.5 months (95% CI: 6.2–13.8) in a well-defined, biomarker-selected population of adult patients with KRAS G12C-mutated locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC who had received at least one prior systemic therapy (all 112 efficacy-evaluable patients had received prior platinum-based chemotherapy and anti-PD-(L)1 therapy). This ORR substantially exceeds historical second-line chemotherapy benchmarks (6.7–14% for docetaxel; 23% for docetaxel + ramucirumab) and compares favorably to sotorasib (ORR 36% in the broader population; 31% in the platinum + anti-PD-1/PD-L1 pretreated subset). The safety profile, while notable for high rates of GI toxicity, QTc prolongation, hepatotoxicity, and ILD/pneumonitis, is manageable through labeling, dose modification guidance, and monitoring, and is acceptable in the context of a uniformly fatal, incurable disease with significant unmet need. The evidence meets the statutory standard for accelerated approval under 21 CFR 314.510, with ORR and DOR as surrogates reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. A confirmatory trial (Study 849-012) is required to verify clinical benefit. Dose optimization remains an outstanding concern but is addressable via a postmarketing requirement rather than a Complete Response Letter.
key_concerns: Single-arm, non-randomized trial design precludes direct causal attribution of benefit and prevents formal comparison of toxicity burden versus standard of care; no randomized OS or PFS data available at time of submission.

ORR and DOR are surrogate endpoints; clinical benefit (OS, PFS) has not yet been verified in a randomized confirmatory trial — accelerated approval pathway is appropriate but verification is mandatory.

Dose optimization: 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, suggesting the 600 mg BID dose may not be optimally tolerated; limited dose-ranging data were submitted and no alternative dose was formally evaluated for non-inferior efficacy with improved tolerability.

Fatal adverse reactions in 11% of patients (pneumonia 3.4%, respiratory failure 1.7%, sudden death 1.7%, cardiac failure 0.9%, pulmonary hemorrhage 0.9%) in a population with advanced cancer — causality attribution is complex but warrants careful labeling.

QTc prolongation (6% with average QTc ≥501 ms; 11% with increase ≥60 ms from baseline) represents a clinically significant cardiac safety signal requiring robust monitoring guidance and labeling warnings.

Plasma companion diagnostic (RESOLUTION ctDx FIRST) has a PPA of only ~63–65% versus tissue testing, meaning up to 37% of tissue-positive patients would be missed; reflex to tissue testing must be clearly mandated in labeling.

Inspectional findings at Site #811 (unreported SAEs: sepsis, DVT, seizure; failure to reconsent 3 patients after protocol amendment) introduce minor data integrity concerns, though overall trial conduct appears adequate.
No overall survival benefit demonstrated at time of submission; OS data are immature and the single-arm design does not permit OS attribution to adagrasib versus subsequent therapies.
Subgroup analyses (e.g., by prior lines of therapy, PD-L1 status, STK11/KEAP1 co-mutation status) are not fully characterized, limiting understanding of which patients derive the most benefit.

deficiencies.description: Unverified clinical benefit via surrogate endpoint only: The pivotal evidence rests entirely on ORR (43%) and DOR (8.5 months) from a single-arm, non-randomized expansion cohort (Study 849-001/KRYSTAL-1). No randomized data confirming improvement in overall survival or progression-free survival are available. While ORR/DOR are acceptable surrogates for accelerated approval in NSCLC per FDA guidance, the clinical benefit remains unverified and a confirmatory randomized trial (Study 849-012) must be completed and submitted as a postmarketing requirement. This deficiency is not blocking under the accelerated approval framework — it is the defining condition of that pathway — but it must be tracked as a PMR.

Dose not optimized at time of approval: The 600 mg BID dose was selected without adequate dose-ranging evaluation of alternative doses for efficacy-safety trade-off. With 82% of patients requiring dose interruption or reduction and a high burden of GI toxicity, QTc prolongation, and hepatotoxicity, there is a reasonable concern that the approved dose may not represent the optimal benefit-risk balance. The exposure-response analyses submitted do not definitively establish that 600 mg BID is the minimum effective dose. A dose optimization study is required as a postmarketing requirement (PMR), not a Complete Response Letter condition, as the current dose does demonstrate meaningful efficacy in a life-threatening disease with unmet need.

Plasma companion diagnostic (RESOLUTION ctDx FIRST) has insufficient sensitivity (PPA ~63–65% vs. tissue CTA) to serve as a standalone diagnostic: approximately 37% of tissue-positive patients would be missed if plasma testing alone were used. Labeling must mandate reflex to tissue testing for plasma-negative results. This is a labeling/CDx issue addressable without a CRL for the drug itself, provided the labeling and CDx approval conditions are appropriately structured.

blind_positions.summary: Adagrasib (MRTX849) is a covalent, irreversible KRAS G12C inhibitor with a well-characterized nonclinical pharmacology package demonstrating high target selectivity and robust in vitro/in vivo anti-tumor activity in KRAS G12C-mutant models. The nonclinical safety program is broadly adequate for an advanced cancer indication under ICH S9 principles. Key toxicological findings (GI toxicity, hepatotoxicity, cardiac/pulmonary findings, reproductive organ effects, phospholipidosis-like changes) are consistent with and predictive of the clinical safety profile observed in Study 849-001. The proposed 600 mg BID dose was not optimally characterized from a dose-optimization standpoint consistent with Project Optimus expectations — no alternative dose levels were formally evaluated in a comparative efficacy/safety framework prior to NDA submission — and 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, signaling that the dose may not be at the therapeutic optimum. This is a significant concern but is addressable via a postmarketing requirement (PMR) for dose optimization rather than a blocking deficiency, given the life-threatening indication, acceptable safety manageability through labeling, and the absence of irreversible or catastrophic nonclinical safety signals that would preclude approval. Overall, from a nonclinical/toxicology perspective, the application is conditionally approvable with a mandatory dose-optimization PMR.
key_concerns: Dose not optimized per Project Optimus principles: 600 mg BID was selected without formal comparative evaluation of alternative doses for efficacy/safety trade-off; 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, strongly suggesting the dose is above the therapeutic optimum for many patients.

Phospholipidosis-like findings (foamy macrophage infiltration, macrophage vacuolation) observed in multiple tissues in both rats and dogs across repeat-dose studies; clinical significance in humans is unknown and long-term consequences are uncharacterized.

Cardiac toxicity signals in nonclinical studies: subacute myocardial necrosis in one dog at 25 mg/kg; diffuse myocardial microvesicular vacuolation and mortality in rats at 300 mg/kg (~1.5x human AUC); these correlate with clinical QTc prolongation (20% incidence ≥Grade 1; 6% with QTc ≥501 ms) and fatal cardiac events (cardiac failure 0.9%, sudden death 1.7%).

Pulmonary toxicity in both species (foamy macrophage infiltration, epithelial vacuolation in alveoli) at exposures near or overlapping clinical exposures; correlates with clinical ILD/pneumonitis (4.1%, including one fatal case) and pneumonia (3.4% fatal).

Reproductive organ toxicity in male and female rats and dogs at exposures approaching or modestly exceeding clinical exposures; adagrasib accumulates 2-3x in male reproductive tissues; fertility studies not conducted (acceptable under ICH S9 for advanced cancer, but labeling must adequately reflect risk).

Genotoxicity: equivocal in vitro micronucleus screening results for major metabolites M11 and M68 (increases in micronuclei up to limit of cytotoxicity, above historical control but not statistically significant); definitive GLP genotoxicity assays not conducted for these metabolites; adagrasib itself is not genotoxic.

hERG IC50 of 3.8 µM (~48x free Cmax) provides some in vitro reassurance, but clinical QTc prolongation is prominent and not fully explained by hERG inhibition alone, suggesting additional mechanisms (e.g., off-target receptor interactions at serotonin 5HT1A/1B, muscarinic M2, alpha-1A adrenergic receptors identified in secondary pharmacology screen).
No carcinogenicity studies conducted — acceptable under ICH S9 for advanced cancer indication.

Embryo-fetal development: no clear teratogenic signal at non-maternally toxic doses in rats or rabbits; embryo-fetal toxicity warning not included in label, which is appropriate given the data, but contraception labeling must be robust.

blind_positions.summary: Adagrasib (MRTX849) at 600 mg BID demonstrates a pharmacologically coherent exposure–response relationship for both efficacy (ORR, PFS, OS vs. Cmin,Week2-6) and key toxicities (GI events, hepatotoxicity, QTc vs. Cmax,ss). The popPK model is adequately characterized with acceptable goodness-of-fit. However, from a Clinical Pharmacology standpoint, the 600 mg BID dose was selected with limited exploration of alternative dose levels in the expansion cohort, and the high rate of dose reductions/interruptions (82%) signals that the approved dose may sit on a steep portion of the toxicity E-R curve without a corresponding steep efficacy E-R slope — a classic dose-optimization concern consistent with Project Optimus principles. DDI liability is substantial (strong CYP3A4 time-dependent inhibitor and inducer, P-gp/BCRP inhibitor), and hepatic impairment dosing guidance required PBPK modeling due to the absence of a complete dedicated clinical study at steady state. QTc prolongation (6% with average QTcF ≥501 ms; 11% with ΔQTcF ≥60 ms) is clinically meaningful and exceeds what the in vitro hERG margin alone would predict, suggesting additional mechanisms. These issues are addressable through labeling and a dose-optimization PMR rather than a Complete Response Letter, supporting a conditional (accelerated approval) recommendation.
key_concerns: Dose not optimized per Project Optimus principles: 82% of patients required dose reduction or interruption, yet only 600 mg BID was evaluated in the expansion cohort (Cohort A); no randomized dose-comparison arm was conducted prior to NDA submission, leaving uncertainty about whether a lower dose (e.g., 400 mg BID or 600 mg QD) could preserve efficacy with improved tolerability.

Exposure–response for efficacy (ORR/PFS/OS vs. Cmin,Week2-6) shows a relatively flat plateau at exposures achieved by most patients at 600 mg BID, while the toxicity E-R (GI events, hepatotoxicity vs. Cmax,ss) shows a steeper positive slope — this asymmetry supports the hypothesis that dose reduction could reduce toxicity without proportional loss of efficacy, but this has not been prospectively tested.

QTc prolongation is disproportionate to the in vitro hERG margin (~48-fold at free Cmax): 6% of patients had mean QTcF ≥501 ms and 11% had ΔQTcF ≥60 ms, suggesting additional QT mechanisms (e.g., hERG trafficking inhibition, metabolite contribution, or off-target ion channel effects) that are not fully characterized. A thorough QT/QTc study or concentration-QTc analysis from the clinical dataset is needed.

Strong CYP3A4 time-dependent inhibition (TDI) AND net induction at steady state creates a complex, bidirectional DDI profile. PBPK-predicted interactions with sensitive CYP3A4 substrates, CYP2D6 substrates, CYP2C9 substrates, and P-gp/BCRP substrates (e.g., rosuvastatin) are based on modeling rather than dedicated clinical DDI studies for several key substrate classes, introducing uncertainty in labeling recommendations.

Hepatic impairment dosing: the dedicated hepatic impairment study provided single-dose data only; steady-state exposures in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment were extrapolated via PBPK modeling (Simcyp V21). The FDA reviewer's refined model and the applicant's model showed concordant directional predictions but with sensitivity to CYP3A4 abundance assumptions and CYP2C8 contribution (20–80% scenarios). Steady-state clinical data in hepatic impairment patients are absent.

Renal impairment: adagrasib is minimally renally excreted, but 36% of NSCLC patients experienced renal impairment as a TEAE; dedicated renal impairment PK data are not described in the review package, and popPK covariate analysis adequacy for this subgroup requires confirmation.

Bioanalytical bridging between the capsule formulation used in early-phase studies and the 200 mg tablet commercial formulation relies on a PK bridging study; while the review notes acceptable bridging, the relative bioavailability confidence interval boundaries and food-effect magnitude should be confirmed in labeling.

The E-R analysis for efficacy used Cmin,Week2-6 as the exposure metric in only 118 patients — a relatively small dataset for robust E-R modeling — and the sensitivity analyses using Cave showed consistent but not identical conclusions, leaving residual uncertainty about the optimal PK driver of efficacy.

blind_positions.summary: From a biostatistics perspective, the primary evidence supporting accelerated approval of adagrasib (KRAZATI) rests on a single-arm, open-label, multicohort expansion study (KRYSTAL-1/Study 849-001) in 112 evaluable patients with KRAS G12C-mutated locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC who had received at least one prior systemic therapy. The primary endpoint — ORR by BICR per RECIST v1.1 — yielded 43% (95% CI: 34%, 53%), with a median DOR of 8.5 months (95% CI: 6.2, 13.8). These results are statistically coherent and clinically meaningful for an accelerated approval pathway in a biomarker-selected population with high unmet need. The single-arm design, absence of a randomized control, and reliance on ORR as a surrogate endpoint are inherent limitations but are acceptable under 21 CFR 314.510 given the disease context and regulatory precedent. Key statistical concerns — including the absence of multiplicity control across secondary endpoints, informative censoring risk in DOR, and the immature OS data — are real but do not individually rise to the level of a blocking deficiency for an accelerated approval. A dose-optimization PMR is warranted given the high rate of dose modifications (82%) and the limited exploration of alternative dosing regimens, which has implications for the exposure-response analyses underpinning the chosen dose.
key_concerns: Single-arm design with no randomized control arm: ORR of 43% (95% CI: 34–53%) is interpretable against historical benchmarks (docetaxel ORR ~7–14%; sotorasib ORR 36%), but absence of concurrent control limits causal inference and precludes formal hypothesis testing with type I error control.

No pre-specified alpha-spending or multiplicity adjustment across secondary endpoints (DOR, PFS, OS): these are reported descriptively and cannot be interpreted as confirmatory. PFS (median not reported in executive summary) and OS (immature at data cutoff) are exploratory only.

DOR estimate of 8.5 months (95% CI: 6.2–13.8) is based on a subset of 48 responders (43% of 112); the wide upper CI bound and the fact that 58% had DOR ≥6 months suggest durability but with substantial uncertainty given the small responder denominator.

Informative censoring risk in DOR and PFS: patients who discontinued due to toxicity (13% permanent discontinuation; 82% dose modification) may have been censored non-randomly, potentially inflating DOR estimates.

Exposure-response (E-R) analyses used to justify the 600 mg BID dose are based on observational PK data from a single-arm trial with substantial dose modifications; 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, meaning the 'as-treated' exposure distribution is heterogeneous and the E-R relationship for efficacy (ORR vs. Cmin,Week2-6) is derived from a confounded dataset.

The primary efficacy population (n=112) is modest in size; while adequate for a single-arm accelerated approval, the point estimate precision (CI width of ~19 percentage points) means the true ORR could be as low as 34%, which is only marginally above sotorasib's lower CI bound.

120-day safety update data cutoff (October 15, 2021) was used for updated DOR and response duration figures (FDA Figure 7, FDA Figure 11), but it is not entirely clear whether the primary ORR analysis and the 120-day update used identical analysis populations and BICR reads — any discordance would require reconciliation.

OSI findings at Site #811 (3 unreported AEs: sepsis, DVT, seizure; 1 unreported concomitant medication) were incorporated post-hoc into the safety dataset; it is not documented whether these findings affected the efficacy-evaluable population or BICR assessments, introducing a minor data integrity concern.

Subgroup analyses of ORR (Applicant Figure 6) are exploratory and uncontrolled for multiplicity; no formal interaction testing was performed, and the small subgroup sizes preclude reliable inference about differential treatment effects across demographic or disease subgroups.

deficiencies.description: Absence of a randomized controlled trial: the entire efficacy case rests on a single-arm cohort (n=112). While acceptable for accelerated approval under 21 CFR 314.510, the ORR-based surrogate has not been validated as predicting OS benefit in KRAS G12C NSCLC, and no confirmatory randomized trial data are available at the time of this NDA. This is a structural limitation of the evidence package that must be addressed via a postmarketing requirement (PMR) to verify clinical benefit.

Dose not optimized at time of NDA submission: 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, yet only the 600 mg BID dose was evaluated in the pivotal cohort. The exposure-response analyses supporting this dose are derived from a confounded, single-arm dataset with heterogeneous as-treated exposures. The sponsor has not prospectively evaluated alternative dosing regimens. This does not block approval but requires a formal dose-optimization PMR (already noted by FDA) to determine whether a lower dose provides comparable efficacy with improved tolerability.

Informative censoring in DOR and PFS: the high rate of treatment discontinuation due to adverse events (13% permanent discontinuation; 82% dose modification) creates a plausible mechanism for non-random censoring in time-to-event analyses. No sensitivity analyses (e.g., worst-case imputation, tipping-point analysis) were presented to assess the robustness of the DOR estimate of 8.5 months. This is a reviewable deficiency addressable by requiring sensitivity analyses as part of the confirmatory PMR dataset.

blind_positions.summary: From a CMC (Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls) perspective, adagrasib (KRAZATI, NDA 216340) is a small-molecule oral tablet (200 mg) — a relatively straightforward solid oral dosage form compared to biologics or ADCs. The case package contains limited CMC-specific detail, but the information available (Table 9: Summary of Adagrasib Drug Impurities; references to OPQ review; no flagged facility inspection failures; standard NME small-molecule manufacturing) does not reveal any blocking CMC deficiency. The impurity profile was characterized and summarized (Table 9), and the OPQ review is referenced without identified critical deficiencies. The product quality section notes no clinical microbiology concerns. One reviewable issue is the limited transparency in the case package regarding long-term stability data, process validation at commercial scale, and the full impurity control strategy — these are standard CMC commitments expected for an accelerated approval NME and are appropriately addressed via post-marketing commitments rather than a CRL. Overall, the CMC bar for a small-molecule tablet is met on the available evidence, with standard post-approval stability and process validation commitments expected.
key_concerns: Limited CMC detail in the case package regarding long-term ICH Q1 stability data at commercial scale — accelerated and real-time stability data adequacy cannot be fully confirmed from the redacted review package.

Table 9 (Summary of Adagrasib Drug Impurities) is referenced but not fully reproduced in the available package; the adequacy of impurity identification, qualification thresholds (ICH Q3A/Q3B), and control limits cannot be independently verified from this document alone.
Process validation comparability between Phase I/II clinical-grade material and proposed commercial-scale manufacturing is not explicitly addressed in the available case package sections.

No explicit facility inspection outcome (OPQ/facility readiness) is documented in the available package beyond a passing reference to the OPQ review — absence of a documented 'no action indicated' or 'voluntary action indicated' outcome for the drug substance and drug product manufacturing sites is a gap.

Two circulating metabolites (M11 and M68) each exceed 10% of adagrasib-related material in human plasma; while the nonclinical team addressed genotoxicity screening, the CMC control strategy for these metabolites as potential drug-related impurities in the drug substance/product should be confirmed as adequate per ICH Q3A.

deficiencies.description: Inadequate transparency in the case package regarding long-term and accelerated ICH Q1 stability data for the commercial drug product (200 mg tablet). For an NME under accelerated approval, confirmed stability through the proposed shelf life at commercial scale is required. The redacted package does not provide sufficient detail to confirm this bar is met; however, this is a standard PMC-resolvable commitment rather than a blocking issue if OPQ has confirmed data adequacy in the full review.

The impurity control strategy (ICH Q3A for drug substance, ICH Q3B for drug product) is referenced via Table 9 but not fully assessable from the available case package. Qualification of impurities at or above the ICH Q3A identification threshold (0.10%) and reporting threshold must be confirmed. If any impurity exceeds the qualification threshold without adequate toxicological qualification, this could be a blocking issue; on available evidence it is treated as reviewable pending OPQ confirmation.

Process validation at proposed commercial manufacturing scale is not explicitly documented in the available sections of the multi-discipline review. Comparability of clinical trial material to commercial-scale drug substance and drug product must be established per ICH Q10/Q11. This is a standard pre-approval requirement; absence of explicit confirmation in the package is a reviewable gap addressable by OPQ prior to approval action.

key_concerns: Single-arm, non-randomized trial design precludes direct causal attribution of benefit and prevents formal comparison of toxicity burden versus standard of care; no randomized OS or PFS data available at time of submission.

ORR and DOR are surrogate endpoints; clinical benefit (OS, PFS) has not yet been verified in a randomized confirmatory trial — accelerated approval pathway is appropriate but verification is mandatory.

Dose optimization: 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, suggesting the 600 mg BID dose may not be optimally tolerated; limited dose-ranging data were submitted and no alternative dose was formally evaluated for non-inferior efficacy with improved tolerability.

Fatal adverse reactions in 11% of patients (pneumonia 3.4%, respiratory failure 1.7%, sudden death 1.7%, cardiac failure 0.9%, pulmonary hemorrhage 0.9%) in a population with advanced cancer — causality attribution is complex but warrants careful labeling.

QTc prolongation (6% with average QTc ≥501 ms; 11% with increase ≥60 ms from baseline) represents a clinically significant cardiac safety signal requiring robust monitoring guidance and labeling warnings.

Plasma companion diagnostic (RESOLUTION ctDx FIRST) has a PPA of only ~63–65% versus tissue testing, meaning up to 37% of tissue-positive patients would be missed; reflex to tissue testing must be clearly mandated in labeling.

Inspectional findings at Site #811 (unreported SAEs: sepsis, DVT, seizure; failure to reconsent 3 patients after protocol amendment) introduce minor data integrity concerns, though overall trial conduct appears adequate.
No overall survival benefit demonstrated at time of submission; OS data are immature and the single-arm design does not permit OS attribution to adagrasib versus subsequent therapies.
Subgroup analyses (e.g., by prior lines of therapy, PD-L1 status, STK11/KEAP1 co-mutation status) are not fully characterized, limiting understanding of which patients derive the most benefit.

deficiencies.description: Unverified clinical benefit via surrogate endpoint only: The pivotal evidence rests entirely on ORR (43%) and DOR (8.5 months) from a single-arm, non-randomized expansion cohort (Study 849-001/KRYSTAL-1). No randomized data confirming improvement in overall survival or progression-free survival are available. While ORR/DOR are acceptable surrogates for accelerated approval in NSCLC per FDA guidance, the clinical benefit remains unverified and a confirmatory randomized trial (Study 849-012) must be completed and submitted as a postmarketing requirement. This deficiency is not blocking under the accelerated approval framework — it is the defining condition of that pathway — but it must be tracked as a PMR.

Dose not optimized at time of approval: The 600 mg BID dose was selected without adequate dose-ranging evaluation of alternative doses for efficacy-safety trade-off. With 82% of patients requiring dose interruption or reduction and a high burden of GI toxicity, QTc prolongation, and hepatotoxicity, there is a reasonable concern that the approved dose may not represent the optimal benefit-risk balance. The exposure-response analyses submitted do not definitively establish that 600 mg BID is the minimum effective dose. A dose optimization study is required as a postmarketing requirement (PMR), not a Complete Response Letter condition, as the current dose does demonstrate meaningful efficacy in a life-threatening disease with unmet need.

Plasma companion diagnostic (RESOLUTION ctDx FIRST) has insufficient sensitivity (PPA ~63–65% vs. tissue CTA) to serve as a standalone diagnostic: approximately 37% of tissue-positive patients would be missed if plasma testing alone were used. Labeling must mandate reflex to tissue testing for plasma-negative results. This is a labeling/CDx issue addressable without a CRL for the drug itself, provided the labeling and CDx approval conditions are appropriately structured.

final_positions.summary: Adagrasib (MRTX849) is a covalent, irreversible KRAS G12C inhibitor with a well-characterized nonclinical pharmacology package demonstrating high target selectivity and robust in vitro/in vivo anti-tumor activity in KRAS G12C-mutant models. The nonclinical safety program is broadly adequate for an advanced cancer indication under ICH S9 principles. Key toxicological findings (GI toxicity, hepatotoxicity, cardiac/pulmonary findings, reproductive organ effects, phospholipidosis-like changes) are consistent with and predictive of the clinical safety profile observed in Study 849-001. The proposed 600 mg BID dose was not optimally characterized from a dose-optimization standpoint consistent with Project Optimus expectations — no alternative dose levels were formally evaluated in a comparative efficacy/safety framework prior to NDA submission — and 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, signaling that the dose may not be at the therapeutic optimum. This is a significant concern but is addressable via a postmarketing requirement (PMR) for dose optimization rather than a blocking deficiency, given the life-threatening indication, acceptable safety manageability through labeling, and the absence of irreversible or catastrophic nonclinical safety signals that would preclude approval. Overall, from a nonclinical/toxicology perspective, the application is conditionally approvable with a mandatory dose-optimization PMR.
key_concerns: Dose not optimized per Project Optimus principles: 600 mg BID was selected without formal comparative evaluation of alternative doses for efficacy/safety trade-off; 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, strongly suggesting the dose is above the therapeutic optimum for many patients.

Phospholipidosis-like findings (foamy macrophage infiltration, macrophage vacuolation) observed in multiple tissues in both rats and dogs across repeat-dose studies; clinical significance in humans is unknown and long-term consequences are uncharacterized.

Cardiac toxicity signals in nonclinical studies: subacute myocardial necrosis in one dog at 25 mg/kg; diffuse myocardial microvesicular vacuolation and mortality in rats at 300 mg/kg (~1.5x human AUC); these correlate with clinical QTc prolongation (20% incidence ≥Grade 1; 6% with QTc ≥501 ms) and fatal cardiac events (cardiac failure 0.9%, sudden death 1.7%).

Pulmonary toxicity in both species (foamy macrophage infiltration, epithelial vacuolation in alveoli) at exposures near or overlapping clinical exposures; correlates with clinical ILD/pneumonitis (4.1%, including one fatal case) and pneumonia (3.4% fatal).

Reproductive organ toxicity in male and female rats and dogs at exposures approaching or modestly exceeding clinical exposures; adagrasib accumulates 2-3x in male reproductive tissues; fertility studies not conducted (acceptable under ICH S9 for advanced cancer, but labeling must adequately reflect risk).

Genotoxicity: equivocal in vitro micronucleus screening results for major metabolites M11 and M68 (increases in micronuclei up to limit of cytotoxicity, above historical control but not statistically significant); definitive GLP genotoxicity assays not conducted for these metabolites; adagrasib itself is not genotoxic.

hERG IC50 of 3.8 µM (~48x free Cmax) provides some in vitro reassurance, but clinical QTc prolongation is prominent and not fully explained by hERG inhibition alone, suggesting additional mechanisms (e.g., off-target receptor interactions at serotonin 5HT1A/1B, muscarinic M2, alpha-1A adrenergic receptors identified in secondary pharmacology screen).
No carcinogenicity studies conducted — acceptable under ICH S9 for advanced cancer indication.

Embryo-fetal development: no clear teratogenic signal at non-maternally toxic doses in rats or rabbits; embryo-fetal toxicity warning not included in label, which is appropriate given the data, but contraception labeling must be robust.

final_positions.summary: Adagrasib (MRTX849) at 600 mg BID demonstrates a pharmacologically coherent exposure–response relationship for both efficacy (ORR, PFS, OS vs. Cmin,Week2-6) and key toxicities (GI events, hepatotoxicity, QTc vs. Cmax,ss). The popPK model is adequately characterized with acceptable goodness-of-fit. However, from a Clinical Pharmacology standpoint, the 600 mg BID dose was selected with limited exploration of alternative dose levels in the expansion cohort, and the high rate of dose reductions/interruptions (82%) signals that the approved dose may sit on a steep portion of the toxicity E-R curve without a corresponding steep efficacy E-R slope — a classic dose-optimization concern consistent with Project Optimus principles. DDI liability is substantial (strong CYP3A4 time-dependent inhibitor and inducer, P-gp/BCRP inhibitor), and hepatic impairment dosing guidance required PBPK modeling due to the absence of a complete dedicated clinical study at steady state. QTc prolongation (6% with average QTcF ≥501 ms; 11% with ΔQTcF ≥60 ms) is clinically meaningful and exceeds what the in vitro hERG margin alone would predict, suggesting additional mechanisms. These issues are addressable through labeling and a dose-optimization PMR rather than a Complete Response Letter, supporting a conditional (accelerated approval) recommendation.
key_concerns: Dose not optimized per Project Optimus principles: 82% of patients required dose reduction or interruption, yet only 600 mg BID was evaluated in the expansion cohort (Cohort A); no randomized dose-comparison arm was conducted prior to NDA submission, leaving uncertainty about whether a lower dose (e.g., 400 mg BID or 600 mg QD) could preserve efficacy with improved tolerability.

Exposure–response for efficacy (ORR/PFS/OS vs. Cmin,Week2-6) shows a relatively flat plateau at exposures achieved by most patients at 600 mg BID, while the toxicity E-R (GI events, hepatotoxicity vs. Cmax,ss) shows a steeper positive slope — this asymmetry supports the hypothesis that dose reduction could reduce toxicity without proportional loss of efficacy, but this has not been prospectively tested.

QTc prolongation is disproportionate to the in vitro hERG margin (~48-fold at free Cmax): 6% of patients had mean QTcF ≥501 ms and 11% had ΔQTcF ≥60 ms, suggesting additional QT mechanisms (e.g., hERG trafficking inhibition, metabolite contribution, or off-target ion channel effects) that are not fully characterized. A thorough QT/QTc study or concentration-QTc analysis from the clinical dataset is needed.

Strong CYP3A4 time-dependent inhibition (TDI) AND net induction at steady state creates a complex, bidirectional DDI profile. PBPK-predicted interactions with sensitive CYP3A4 substrates, CYP2D6 substrates, CYP2C9 substrates, and P-gp/BCRP substrates (e.g., rosuvastatin) are based on modeling rather than dedicated clinical DDI studies for several key substrate classes, introducing uncertainty in labeling recommendations.

Hepatic impairment dosing: the dedicated hepatic impairment study provided single-dose data only; steady-state exposures in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment were extrapolated via PBPK modeling (Simcyp V21). The FDA reviewer's refined model and the applicant's model showed concordant directional predictions but with sensitivity to CYP3A4 abundance assumptions and CYP2C8 contribution (20–80% scenarios). Steady-state clinical data in hepatic impairment patients are absent.

Renal impairment: adagrasib is minimally renally excreted, but 36% of NSCLC patients experienced renal impairment as a TEAE; dedicated renal impairment PK data are not described in the review package, and popPK covariate analysis adequacy for this subgroup requires confirmation.

Bioanalytical bridging between the capsule formulation used in early-phase studies and the 200 mg tablet commercial formulation relies on a PK bridging study; while the review notes acceptable bridging, the relative bioavailability confidence interval boundaries and food-effect magnitude should be confirmed in labeling.

The E-R analysis for efficacy used Cmin,Week2-6 as the exposure metric in only 118 patients — a relatively small dataset for robust E-R modeling — and the sensitivity analyses using Cave showed consistent but not identical conclusions, leaving residual uncertainty about the optimal PK driver of efficacy.

final_positions.summary: From a biostatistics perspective, the primary evidence supporting accelerated approval of adagrasib (KRAZATI) rests on a single-arm, open-label, multicohort expansion study (KRYSTAL-1/Study 849-001) in 112 evaluable patients with KRAS G12C-mutated locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC who had received at least one prior systemic therapy. The primary endpoint — ORR by BICR per RECIST v1.1 — yielded 43% (95% CI: 34%, 53%), with a median DOR of 8.5 months (95% CI: 6.2, 13.8). These results are statistically coherent and clinically meaningful for an accelerated approval pathway in a biomarker-selected population with high unmet need. The single-arm design, absence of a randomized control, and reliance on ORR as a surrogate endpoint are inherent limitations but are acceptable under 21 CFR 314.510 given the disease context and regulatory precedent. Key statistical concerns — including the absence of multiplicity control across secondary endpoints, informative censoring risk in DOR, and the immature OS data — are real but do not individually rise to the level of a blocking deficiency for an accelerated approval. A dose-optimization PMR is warranted given the high rate of dose modifications (82%) and the limited exploration of alternative dosing regimens, which has implications for the exposure-response analyses underpinning the chosen dose.
key_concerns: Single-arm design with no randomized control arm: ORR of 43% (95% CI: 34–53%) is interpretable against historical benchmarks (docetaxel ORR ~7–14%; sotorasib ORR 36%), but absence of concurrent control limits causal inference and precludes formal hypothesis testing with type I error control.

No pre-specified alpha-spending or multiplicity adjustment across secondary endpoints (DOR, PFS, OS): these are reported descriptively and cannot be interpreted as confirmatory. PFS (median not reported in executive summary) and OS (immature at data cutoff) are exploratory only.

DOR estimate of 8.5 months (95% CI: 6.2–13.8) is based on a subset of 48 responders (43% of 112); the wide upper CI bound and the fact that 58% had DOR ≥6 months suggest durability but with substantial uncertainty given the small responder denominator.

Informative censoring risk in DOR and PFS: patients who discontinued due to toxicity (13% permanent discontinuation; 82% dose modification) may have been censored non-randomly, potentially inflating DOR estimates.

Exposure-response (E-R) analyses used to justify the 600 mg BID dose are based on observational PK data from a single-arm trial with substantial dose modifications; 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, meaning the 'as-treated' exposure distribution is heterogeneous and the E-R relationship for efficacy (ORR vs. Cmin,Week2-6) is derived from a confounded dataset.

The primary efficacy population (n=112) is modest in size; while adequate for a single-arm accelerated approval, the point estimate precision (CI width of ~19 percentage points) means the true ORR could be as low as 34%, which is only marginally above sotorasib's lower CI bound.

120-day safety update data cutoff (October 15, 2021) was used for updated DOR and response duration figures (FDA Figure 7, FDA Figure 11), but it is not entirely clear whether the primary ORR analysis and the 120-day update used identical analysis populations and BICR reads — any discordance would require reconciliation.

OSI findings at Site #811 (3 unreported AEs: sepsis, DVT, seizure; 1 unreported concomitant medication) were incorporated post-hoc into the safety dataset; it is not documented whether these findings affected the efficacy-evaluable population or BICR assessments, introducing a minor data integrity concern.

Subgroup analyses of ORR (Applicant Figure 6) are exploratory and uncontrolled for multiplicity; no formal interaction testing was performed, and the small subgroup sizes preclude reliable inference about differential treatment effects across demographic or disease subgroups.

deficiencies.description: Absence of a randomized controlled trial: the entire efficacy case rests on a single-arm cohort (n=112). While acceptable for accelerated approval under 21 CFR 314.510, the ORR-based surrogate has not been validated as predicting OS benefit in KRAS G12C NSCLC, and no confirmatory randomized trial data are available at the time of this NDA. This is a structural limitation of the evidence package that must be addressed via a postmarketing requirement (PMR) to verify clinical benefit.

Dose not optimized at time of NDA submission: 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, yet only the 600 mg BID dose was evaluated in the pivotal cohort. The exposure-response analyses supporting this dose are derived from a confounded, single-arm dataset with heterogeneous as-treated exposures. The sponsor has not prospectively evaluated alternative dosing regimens. This does not block approval but requires a formal dose-optimization PMR (already noted by FDA) to determine whether a lower dose provides comparable efficacy with improved tolerability.

Informative censoring in DOR and PFS: the high rate of treatment discontinuation due to adverse events (13% permanent discontinuation; 82% dose modification) creates a plausible mechanism for non-random censoring in time-to-event analyses. No sensitivity analyses (e.g., worst-case imputation, tipping-point analysis) were presented to assess the robustness of the DOR estimate of 8.5 months. This is a reviewable deficiency addressable by requiring sensitivity analyses as part of the confirmatory PMR dataset.

final_positions.summary: From a CMC (Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls) perspective, adagrasib (KRAZATI, NDA 216340) is a small-molecule oral tablet (200 mg) — a relatively straightforward solid oral dosage form compared to biologics or ADCs. The case package contains limited CMC-specific detail, but the information available (Table 9: Summary of Adagrasib Drug Impurities; references to OPQ review; no flagged facility inspection failures; standard NME small-molecule manufacturing) does not reveal any blocking CMC deficiency. The impurity profile was characterized and summarized (Table 9), and the OPQ review is referenced without identified critical deficiencies. The product quality section notes no clinical microbiology concerns. One reviewable issue is the limited transparency in the case package regarding long-term stability data, process validation at commercial scale, and the full impurity control strategy — these are standard CMC commitments expected for an accelerated approval NME and are appropriately addressed via post-marketing commitments rather than a CRL. Overall, the CMC bar for a small-molecule tablet is met on the available evidence, with standard post-approval stability and process validation commitments expected.
key_concerns: Limited CMC detail in the case package regarding long-term ICH Q1 stability data at commercial scale — accelerated and real-time stability data adequacy cannot be fully confirmed from the redacted review package.

Table 9 (Summary of Adagrasib Drug Impurities) is referenced but not fully reproduced in the available package; the adequacy of impurity identification, qualification thresholds (ICH Q3A/Q3B), and control limits cannot be independently verified from this document alone.
Process validation comparability between Phase I/II clinical-grade material and proposed commercial-scale manufacturing is not explicitly addressed in the available case package sections.

No explicit facility inspection outcome (OPQ/facility readiness) is documented in the available package beyond a passing reference to the OPQ review — absence of a documented 'no action indicated' or 'voluntary action indicated' outcome for the drug substance and drug product manufacturing sites is a gap.

Two circulating metabolites (M11 and M68) each exceed 10% of adagrasib-related material in human plasma; while the nonclinical team addressed genotoxicity screening, the CMC control strategy for these metabolites as potential drug-related impurities in the drug substance/product should be confirmed as adequate per ICH Q3A.

deficiencies.description: Inadequate transparency in the case package regarding long-term and accelerated ICH Q1 stability data for the commercial drug product (200 mg tablet). For an NME under accelerated approval, confirmed stability through the proposed shelf life at commercial scale is required. The redacted package does not provide sufficient detail to confirm this bar is met; however, this is a standard PMC-resolvable commitment rather than a blocking issue if OPQ has confirmed data adequacy in the full review.

The impurity control strategy (ICH Q3A for drug substance, ICH Q3B for drug product) is referenced via Table 9 but not fully assessable from the available case package. Qualification of impurities at or above the ICH Q3A identification threshold (0.10%) and reporting threshold must be confirmed. If any impurity exceeds the qualification threshold without adequate toxicological qualification, this could be a blocking issue; on available evidence it is treated as reviewable pending OPQ confirmation.

Process validation at proposed commercial manufacturing scale is not explicitly documented in the available sections of the multi-discipline review. Comparability of clinical trial material to commercial-scale drug substance and drug product must be established per ICH Q10/Q11. This is a standard pre-approval requirement; absence of explicit confirmation in the package is a reviewable gap addressable by OPQ prior to approval action.

major_deficiencies.description: Absence of a randomized confirmatory trial at submission: The pivotal evidence rests solely on a single-arm trial (KRYSTAL-1) with ORR (43%, 95% CI: 34–53%) and DOR (median 8.5 months) as surrogate endpoints. No OS or PFS data from a randomized trial are available at the time of submission. Under accelerated approval (21 CFR 314.510), a post-marketing confirmatory trial (KRYSTAL-12) is required to verify clinical benefit; failure to initiate or complete this trial in a timely manner would constitute grounds for withdrawal of approval.

Dose optimization inadequately explored prior to NDA submission (Project Optimus): At the proposed 600 mg BID dose, 82% of patients required dose interruption or reduction, indicating the submitted dose may not represent the optimal benefit-risk balance. No systematic dose-ranging or dose-optimization study was conducted prior to submission in alignment with FDA's Project Optimus framework. The sponsor must provide a prospective dose-optimization plan or data demonstrating that 600 mg BID is the minimally efficacious dose with an acceptable tolerability profile, or propose an alternative dose supported by exposure-response analyses.

QTc prolongation risk not fully characterized for labeling and risk management: 6% of patients experienced average QTc ≥501 ms and 11% had an increase ≥60 ms from baseline, representing a clinically significant cardiac safety signal. Although the hERG IC50 of 3.8 µM provides an approximately 48-fold margin over free Cmax, the clinical QTc data are prominent. The current submission requires a thorough QTc characterization, including concentration-QTc modeling, to support definitive Warnings and Precautions language, contraindications for concomitant QT-prolonging agents, and ECG monitoring guidance adequate to protect patients.

Plasma companion diagnostic (RESOLUTION ctDx FIRST) sensitivity limitations inadequately addressed in labeling: The plasma CDx demonstrates a positive predictive agreement (PPA) of only ~63–65% relative to tissue testing, meaning a substantial proportion of KRAS G12C-positive patients may be missed if plasma testing alone is used. The submission does not include sufficiently clear labeling language mandating reflex to tissue testing for plasma-negative results, creating a risk that eligible patients will be denied access or that patients without the target mutation will be treated. The reflex testing algorithm must be explicitly codified in the approved labeling and CDx labeling.

Hepatotoxicity risk management inadequately defined: A 37% overall incidence of hepatotoxicity (7% Grade 3/4) in the primary safety population requires more than a Warnings and Precautions statement. The submission lacks a fully specified liver function monitoring schedule, clear dose-modification rules tied to hepatotoxicity grade, and criteria for permanent discontinuation. Without these elements codified in labeling, the risk cannot be considered adequately managed for approval.

Drug-drug interaction (DDI) liability incompletely characterized for labeling: Adagrasib is a time-dependent CYP3A4 inhibitor and affects multiple transporters (P-gp, BCRP, OATP). The DDI characterization relies substantially on PBPK modeling without sufficient clinical validation for all key interaction pairs. Labeling guidance on co-administration with sensitive CYP3A4 substrates, strong CYP3A4 inducers/inhibitors, and transporter substrates is not yet adequate to ensure safe use in the polypharmacy-heavy NSCLC population.

Drug substance impurity characterization incomplete: Table 9 of the submission lists drug substance impurities, but critical details are redacted in the reviewed package. OPQ must confirm that all identified impurities are qualified within ICH Q3A thresholds or are supported by adequate toxicological justification before approval can be granted. Unresolved impurity qualification represents a chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) deficiency that must be resolved.
